summary: 1933 Aermotor cab from Split Creek Point, Valley County, Idaho. The steel tower came down in 2008; the cab is now at the Central Idaho Historical Museum in McCall.

facts.design: Aermotor 7x7 observation cab on a 72-foot open steel tower
facts.status_note: The steel tower was dismantled in 2008. The lookout cab stands at the Central Idaho Historical Museum in McCall, Idaho, and may be toured.
facts.agency: Central Idaho Historical Museum (cab); Payette National Forest is a cooperator on the register entry

access.note: The cab at the McCall museum may be toured. The original summit is reached on foot by trail.

visit.trail_note: Two trails, FST-081 and FST-086, reach the summit. The climbing guide puts the distance from the trailhead at just under 5.0 miles.

events.note: Lookout and residence cabin constructed, per the register
Steel tower dismantled that year, per the register and the 2008 chapter report
Chapter report says 'the Split Creek Point cabin' was intentionally damaged by Forest Service personnel; it does not say whether that was the lookout cab or the residence cabin

evidence.quote: Split Creek Point Lookout and residence cabin were constructed in 1933.

evidence.supports: Aermotor 7x7 cab on a 72-foot open steel tower
evidence.quote: The lookout structure was an Aermotor 7x7 observation cabin atop a 72 foot X-Brace open steel tower.

evidence.supports: tower disassembled 2008; residence cabin stayed at original site
evidence.quote: The lookout tower was disassembled in 2008 with the residence cabin remaining at the original site.

evidence.supports: lookout cab relocated to museum in McCall; may be toured
evidence.quote: The lookout cab was relocated to the Central Idaho Historical Museum in McCall, Idaho and may be toured by visitors.

evidence.quote: US Forest Service - Payette National Forest
the steel tower at Split Creek Point was dismantled.

evidence.quote: The Split Creek Point cabin was also intentionally damaged by FS personnel.

evidence.quote: Its summit is still graced by a cabin built in the 1930s.

evidence.quote: Despite years of neglect, it is still standing strong with straight lines and a functioning roof.
The summit of Split Creek Point is reached by using 2 trails, FST-081 and FST-086.

notes_for_editor: The date the cab was moved is not given by the register, and a search did not find it. The register (2020) says the residence cabin stayed at the original site. The 2016 climbing guide describes a 1930s cabin still on the summit; it may mean the residence cabin, or the lookout cab before it moved. The sources do not settle this. Height: the register says 72 feet and the guide says 75 feet. The record's coordinates and elevation (1,529 m) are the museum's in McCall, not the original summit; the guide gives the summit at about 45.108 N, -115.775 W and 6,628 ft, which belongs to the record for the original site. A search result named a different McCall museum lookout (Sloan's Point); not verified and not used. The 2008 chapter report calls the damaged building 'the Split Creek Point cabin' and does not say whether it was the lookout cab or the residence cabin. The record status standing is kept, with a status_note added because the tower is gone. Fact-check 2026-10-08: the story previously said the report did not name a cabin; it does, so the story now quotes that wording.
